headings.title: Introduction to Adolescent Nutrition
headings.content: Adolescence represents a critical transitional period between childhood and adulthood, marked by rapid physical, psychological, and social development. During this phase, adequate nutrition is paramount not only to support immediate growth spurts but also to lay a solid foundation for lifelong health and future reproductive capabilities. For adolescent girls, this stage is particularly significant due to the impending physiological demands of menstruation and potential future pregnancies. Malnutrition or poor dietary habits established during these formative years can lead to irreversible stunting, delayed puberty, and an increased risk of chronic non-communicable diseases later in life. As nursing professionals in Nigeria, understanding the fundamentals of adolescent nutrition enables us to identify vulnerable populations, advocate for nutritional health, and deliver targeted educational interventions. Nurses play a frontline role in addressing nutritional deficits by bridging the gap between clinical guidelines and community realities. By promoting healthy eating patterns early, we help mitigate public health challenges such as adolescent malnutrition, obesity, and micronutrient deficiencies, thereby improving overall health indices across the country. Comprehensive nutritional care requires looking beyond mere caloric intake to evaluate the quality, frequency, and socio-economic accessibility of the food consumed by young girls.

headings.title: Physiological Changes and Increased Nutritional Demands
headings.content: The adolescent growth spurt brings about dramatic physiological changes, including a rapid increase in height, weight, and skeletal mass, alongside significant hormonal shifts. This accelerated growth demands a higher intake of macro- and micronutrients compared to earlier childhood years. Body composition also undergoes a noticeable transformation; adolescent girls experience a natural increase in body fat percentage, which is a necessary physiological adaptation for reproductive health. Concurrently, the onset of menarche introduces regular blood loss, significantly escalating the daily requirement for specific nutrients, most notably iron. Because energy and nutrient needs peak during peak height velocity, failure to meet these elevated nutritional demands can stunt linear growth and delay sexual maturation. Furthermore, the brain continues to undergo structural remodeling, requiring adequate energy and essential fatty acids for optimal cognitive development and academic performance. Nurses must recognize that these physiological demands are non-negotiable biological requirements. Educational strategies must therefore emphasize nutrient-dense foods rather than restrictive dieting, ensuring that growing girls receive the building blocks necessary for healthy tissue synthesis, hormonal balance, and overall physical maturation during this pivotal window of development.

headings.title: Key Micronutrients: Iron, Calcium, and Folic Acid
headings.content: Micronutrient deficiencies are a major public health concern among adolescent girls, with iron, calcium, and folic acid being of utmost clinical importance. Iron is essential for hemoglobin synthesis and the prevention of iron-deficiency anemia, a condition prevalent among Nigerian teens due to menstrual losses and diets lacking in heme iron. Calcium is critical during adolescence because nearly half of total adult skeletal mass is formed during this decade; inadequate intake predisposes girls to osteoporosis later in life. Folic acid, a B vitamin, is vital for rapid cell division and tissue growth, and establishing sufficient stores during adolescence is crucial for preventing neural tube defects in future pregnancies. To combat these deficiencies, nurses should promote the consumption of locally available nutrient-dense foods such as dark green leafy vegetables, beans, lean meats, and fortified staples. In many clinical settings, routine supplementation programs, such as weekly iron and folic acid supplementation (WIFAS), are implemented to bridge the nutritional gap. Educating adolescent girls and their caregivers on combining iron-rich foods with vitamin C-enhanced sources—such as citrus fruits—greatly improves mineral absorption and overall nutritional status.

headings.title: Macronutrient Balance and Energy Requirements
headings.content: Balancing macronutrients—carbohydrates, proteins, and fats—is fundamental to meeting the high daily energy requirements of growing adolescent girls. Carbohydrates should form the primary source of energy, with an emphasis on complex, fiber-rich sources like whole grains, yams, and plantains that provide sustained energy and support gastrointestinal health. Proteins are equally vital for tissue repair, enzyme synthesis, and structural growth; adequate intake must come from a mix of plant-based proteins (such as legumes and nuts) and animal-based proteins (such as fish, eggs, and poultry) to ensure a complete profile of essential amino acids. Healthy fats are necessary for hormone production, cellular membrane integrity, and the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K). However, nurses must guide adolescents to limit excessive intake of trans fats and refined sugars, which contribute to the rising burden of adolescent obesity and metabolic disorders. Energy requirements vary depending on physical activity levels, meaning sedentary girls require different caloric intakes compared to those engaged in heavy manual labor or sports. Educational messages should focus on portion control, balanced plate models, and avoiding empty-calorie junk foods that displace nutrient-dense meals necessary for optimal adolescent development.

headings.title: Common Nutritional Deficiencies in Nigerian Adolescent Girls
headings.content: In Nigeria, adolescent girls face a high burden of nutritional deficiencies driven by economic constraints, poor dietary diversity, and culturally rooted eating practices. Iron-deficiency anemia remains the most prevalent hematological issue, leading to chronic fatigue, poor concentration in school, and reduced physical work capacity. Protein-energy malnutrition, although more commonly discussed in younger children, manifests among vulnerable adolescent populations as mild stunting, muscle wasting, and compromised immune function. Additionally, micronutrient hidden hunger—characterized by inadequate intakes of vitamin A, zinc, and iodine—impairs immune defense, skin integrity, and thyroid function. Paradoxically, the nutritional landscape is also seeing a surge in overweight and obesity, particularly in urban areas, driven by the consumption of energy-dense, nutrient-poor processed foods and sedentary lifestyles. Nurses encountering these dual burdens of malnutrition must conduct thorough dietary screenings during routine clinic visits. Recognizing clinical signs such as pallor, angular stomatitis, dry skin, and lethargy allows nurses to initiate timely interventions, prescribe appropriate therapeutic or prophylactic supplements, and provide culturally appropriate dietary counseling to both the adolescents and their families.

headings.title: Socio-Cultural Influences on Adolescent Dietary Habits
headings.content: Dietary habits during adolescence are heavily shaped by socio-cultural norms, family dynamics, and peer pressure. In many Nigerian communities, traditional food practices and patriarchal feeding customs may inadvertently disadvantage adolescent girls; for instance, preferential allocation of protein-rich portions to male family members can leave girls with nutrient-deficient meals. Furthermore, modern socio-cultural shifts have popularized Westernized fast foods, leading to a dietary transition away from traditional, nutrient-dense local dishes toward processed, high-sodium, and high-sugar snacks. Peer pressure also heavily dictates body image ideals, prompting many young girls to adopt extreme, unguided weight-loss diets, skipping meals, or fasting, which severely compromises their nutritional status. Nurses must navigate these complex socio-cultural landscapes with cultural competence and sensitivity. Instead of dismissing traditional practices, nurses should leverage positive cultural norms and work closely with family decision-makers and community leaders to advocate for equitable food distribution within the household. Educational sessions should address body image dissatisfaction, promoting positive self-esteem and realistic health goals that align with balanced eating rather than dangerous dietary restrictions.

headings.title: Assessment of Nutritional Status in Clinical Practice
headings.content: Assessing the nutritional status of adolescent girls is a core competency for clinical nurses, requiring a combination of anthropometric, biochemical, clinical, and dietary methods. Anthropometric measurements include recording height, weight, and calculating Body Mass Index (BMI)-for-age percentiles to accurately track growth trajectories and screen for underweight, overweight, or stunting. Clinical assessments involve examining the adolescent for physical signs of malnutrition, such as pale conjunctiva for anemia, brittle hair, skin lesions, and enlarged thyroid glands indicating iodine deficiency. Biochemical assessments, when available through laboratory facilities, involve checking hemoglobin levels, serum ferritin, and other micronutrient panels to confirm suspected deficiencies objectively. Dietary assessment methods, such as 24-hour dietary recalls or food frequency questionnaires, provide insight into habitual food intake and help identify gaps in macronutrient and micronutrient consumption. Nurses must perform these assessments with empathy, maintaining adolescent confidentiality to encourage honest reporting regarding dietary habits and body image concerns. Early and accurate nutritional assessment empowers healthcare providers to catch deviations from normal growth patterns early, thereby preventing long-term systemic complications.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Dietary Counselling
headings.content: Nursing interventions and dietary counselling for adolescent girls must be practical, individualized, and culturally resonant. Nurses should provide guidance centered on the 'food plate' model, encouraging half the plate to be filled with fruits and vegetables, a quarter with whole grains, and a quarter with quality proteins. Counselling sessions must address practical barriers to healthy eating, such as financial constraints, by highlighting affordable, locally available Nigerian foods like beans, groundnuts, local grains, and seasonal vegetables. Interventions should also incorporate health promotion regarding menstrual hygiene and iron supplementation compliance, ensuring girls understand why taking their weekly iron and folic acid tablets is vital for their academic and physical well-being. Furthermore, nurses should actively engage schools, youth clubs, and community centers to conduct group educational workshops that destigmatize nutritional discussions and promote healthy body image. Documentation and follow-up are critical components of care; nurses must re-evaluate anthropometric markers and clinical symptoms during subsequent visits to measure the effectiveness of the dietary plan. Empowering adolescent girls with accurate nutritional knowledge fosters sustainable self-care habits that they will carry into their adult and reproductive lives.
